title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Benchmarking Playbook
author: Priya Shah
body:
Overview

This playbook consolidates the serving runtime reference material: architecture overview, kernel scheduling policies, profiling procedures, benchmarking suite, release-note highlights, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is the canonical starting point for engineers performing performance tuning, incident response, and model onboarding for the Redwood serving runtime.

1) Executive summary
- Goal: ensure predictable, low-latency, cost-efficient inference across hosted, dedicated, and private environments.
- Scope: GPU inference runtime (kernel selection, batching, KV cache management), schedulers (CPU/GPU job placement and preemption), profiling and benchmark tooling, and operational runbooks.

2) Runtime architecture (summary)
- Components:
  - Frontend API gateway: request validation, auth, routing policy (latency vs cost vs region).
  - Router / dispatcher: request classification (chat vs streaming vs embeddings), selects model variant and route.
  - Inference execution layer: model loader, KV cache, tokenizer, execution graph.
  - Kernel selection layer: chooses optimized operators (FP16/INT8/quantized kernels) and fusion kernels based on model + seq-length profile.
  - Batch manager: continuous batching with latency SLO knobs (max-delay-ms, max-batch-size, priority queue).
  - Autoscaler: scales pool size based on queue length, throughput targets and pre-warmed capacity.
  - Observability agents: metrics (Prometheus), traces (Jaeger), and structured logs to ELK.

- Dataflow (high-level): incoming request -> router -> scheduler -> batch manager -> execution on GPU (kernel selection, KV cache lookup, compute) -> postprocess -> response.

- Design constraints and tradeoffs:
  - Latency vs efficiency: small max-delay-ms values reduce batching efficiency but improve p95 latency.
  - Memory isolation vs packing: per-tenant memory reservations avoid noisy-neighbor OOMs but reduce utilization.
  - Quantization compatibility: fallback to higher-precision kernels when quality regressions detected.

3) Kernel scheduling and heuristics
- Objectives: maximize throughput while meeting latency SLOs, avoid starvation, and maintain GPU memory headroom for KV caches.

- Scheduling primitives:
  - Priority queues: interactive (high-priority, low-delay) vs batch (throughput-optimized).
  - Slot allocator: fixed number of concurrent execution slots per GPU to limit collective memory usage.
  - Preemption policy: preempt long-running low-priority batches when high-priority interactive request arrives (graceful cancellation and retry to alternate slot).
  - Affinity rules: model pinning for warm kernels and memory locality (NUMA/GPU topology-aware placement).

- Heuristics and tuning knobs:
  - max-delay-ms (default 6 ms for interactive; configurable per-route).
  - max-batch-size (default 32 for convo models; 128 for embeddings).
  - kv-cache-reservation (bytes) per slot to guarantee OOM-safe operation.
  - kernel-variant-thresholds: switch to quantized kernel only if throughput gain > 2x and eval score delta < configured tolerance.

- Observability for scheduling:
  - Expose queue depth, head-of-line wait time, slot utilization, preemption rate, and per-slot memory allocation.
  - Alerts: queue_depth > 200 for 1m; head_of_line_wait_ms_p95 > SLO_threshold -> oncall.

4) Profiling playbook (how to collect and interpret traces)
- Tools used:
  - GPU: NVIDIA Nsight Systems, nvprof (deprecated on new drivers but available), nvidia-smi sampling.
  - CPU: perf, FlameGraphs (Brendan Gregg), pprof for Go services.
  - Distributed tracing: Jaeger/OTel traces with span annotations for kernel-selection, batch-wait, execution-start, execution-end.
  - Custom: lightweight micro-bench harness (python) that emits per-op timings and memory snapshots.

- Step-by-step profiling procedure:
  1. Reproduce target workload (traffic replay or synthetic generator).
  2. Enable tracing at three levels: control-plane tracing, batch manager timing, and per-kernel timing.
  3. Collect a 5-15 minute Nsight Systems capture for representative peak window (include GPU metrics: SM utilization, memory utilization, PCIe throughput).
  4. Capture pprof CPU profile for the same window and produce flame graphs.
  5. Correlate traces: identify time spent in queue vs kernel execution vs memory copies.
  6. Identify hotspots: long memcpy H2D/D2H, kernel launch overhead, and serialization bottlenecks.
  7. Tune: increase batch-size if kernel time dominates; decrease max-delay-ms if queue wait dominates; consider fused kernels or different memory packing for memcpy hotspots.

- Profiling checklist (quick):
  - Verify driver and CUDA versions match profiling tool requirements.
  - Validate timestamps aligned across traces (NTP).
  - Ensure representative sequence-length distribution.
  - Capture both cold and warm runs (model load penalty vs steady-state).

5) Benchmarking suite (purpose & tests)
- Goals: provide reproducible, comparable performance numbers (latency p50/p95/p99, throughput, memory, cost per token) across model variants, kernels, hardware types, and quantization profiles.

- Test types:
  - Latency microbench: single-request latencies across sequence lengths (16, 64, 256, 1024).
  - Throughput stress: sustained concurrent requests to measure tokens/sec at different batch sizes.
  - Mixed workload: 80/20 interactive vs long-generation mix to measure tail behavior.
  - Embedding sweep: 512/1024/2048-dim embedding throughput and memory.
  - End-to-end cost test: measure tokenized input+output bytes, GPU-hours, and compute unit costs to compute $/1M tokens.

- Benchmark harness features:
  - Config driven (YAML): target model, hardware, sequence distribution, concurrency profile, run-length, warmup iterations.
  - Deterministic workload replay using recorded request traces.
  - Automated result collection: Prometheus scrape + JSON output with p50/p95/p99, token/sec, and GPU utilization.

- Running a canonical benchmark (example):
  1. Checkout benchmark harness repo and select config: configs/llama-2-70b-latency.yaml
  2. Deploy on dedicated cluster with pinned GPUs and zero co-tenancy.
  3. Warm-up: run 300 warmup requests, verify kernel cache warmed.
  4. Run measured window: 10,000 requests at target concurrency.
  5. Collect and publish JSON results to benchmarks bucket and add to Dashboard.

6) Release notes (recent highlights)
- v2026.11.0 (2026-11-10): improved kernel selector to prefer fused attention kernels for decoder-only models; default max-delay-ms reduced to 6ms for interactive routes.
- v2026.08.2 (2026-08-01): added preemption-safe batch rollback to reduce tail latency for high-priority requests.
- v2026.05.0 (2026-05-15): integrated INT8 quantized kernels for Llama-family models with evaluation gating.

7) Known issues and mitigations
- Issue: Occasional head-of-line blocking when many small requests interleave with long-generator streams.
  - Mitigation: enforce strict priority separation, set generator route to lower priority and cap concurrent generator slots.
- Issue: Memory fragmentation on long-running hosts causes intermittent OOMs after weeks of uptime.
  - Mitigation: periodic process recycle and memory compaction jobs; upgrade to driver 525+ where kernel-level improvements reduce fragmentation.
- Issue: Some custom fused kernels show correctness drift on INT8 for rare token patterns.
  - Mitigation: auto-fallback to FP16 kernel for sample rate > 0.05% or on quality regression alerts.

8) Runbooks (operational procedures)
- High latency (p95 spike)
  1. Check global dashboard (per-route latency, queue depth, preemption rate).
  2. If queue_depth > configured threshold: scale up pool (manual step) or increase burst capacity for affected pool.
  3. If preemption rate high: check for runaway long generators; throttle or lower priority.
  4. If kernel execution time increased: run profiling capture (Nsight) on representative host.
  5. Notify serving-runtime oncall and open incident with traces attached.

- GPU OOMs or instability
  1. Identify affected host(s), drain new requests (set read-only).
  2. Collect nvidia-smi topo/status, dmesg, and process list.
  3. If OOM correlates with a specific model, reduce kv-cache-reservation for that slot or reduce max-concurrency.
  4. If memory corruption suspected, repro with controlled harness; escalate to runtime-kernel team.

- Kernel correctness regression (wrong outputs)
  1. Rollback to previous model/kernal variant via route pinning.
  2. Capture deterministic repro trace and file with applied-tests tag.
  3. Run quantization validation suite; if failure confirmed, mark kernel variant as deprecated until patch.

10) Appendices
- SLOs (examples):
  - interactive-route: p50 < 20ms, p95 < 120ms, p99 < 300ms (regional hosted tiers).
  - batch-route (throughput): sustained 2k tokens/sec per GPU at 90% utilization.

- Contact matrix and escalation policy:
  - First line: runtime-oncall (30m target).
  - Second line: kernel-team lead (2h target).
  - Exec: VP Eng for Sev-1 prolonged outages (4h).
